The Lesser scaup (Aythya affinis) is a diving duck that breeds across the boreal wetlands of North America. Freshly laid eggs have an initial wet weight of approximately 51 grams [Ww0 = approximately 51 grams], providing a substantial yolk reserve to sustain embryonic development. Under a stable nest temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 24 days [ab = approximately 24 days], a duration typical of medium-sized anatids. Upon hatching, the precocial duckling weighs approximately 30.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 30.8 grams], a mass sufficient to support immediate mobility and thermoregulation as the brood leaves the nest for open water within hours of hatching.

Growth during the nestling and juvenile phases proceeds rapidly as the ducklings feed on aquatic invertebrates alongside the hen. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C], fledging occurs at approximately 69 days after hatching [tx = approximately 69 days after hatching], at which point the juvenile has attained a wet weight at fledging of approximately 471 grams [Wwx = approximately 471 grams]. Sexual maturation follows shortly afterward, with puberty attained at approximately 120 days after hatching [tp = approximately 120 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C].

Adult body mass in the Lesser scaup exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 730 grams [Wwi = approximately 730 grams], while males grow somewhat larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of approximately 820 grams [Wwi = approximately 820 grams]. This modest size disparity between the sexes is typical of diving ducks and may relate to differential energetic demands between incubating females and territorial males. Despite reaching physiological maturity within its first four months, first successful breeding is deferred considerably: the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1.2 years after hatching [tR = approximately 1.2 years after hatching] at 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C], reflecting the time required to secure a mate, a breeding territory, and sufficient body condition.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a single annual clutch. Under the active metabolic thermal regime of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 10 ducklings per year [Ri = approximately 10 ducklings per year]. Longevity records indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 18.3 years [am = approximately 18.3 years] at the same thermal reference of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C], a considerable duration for a diving duck of this body size and one that permits repeated breeding attempts across many seasons, buffering the population against years of poor recruitment on the northern breeding grounds.
